summary: The Guptas ruled much of northern India during a period of influential mathematics, Sanskrit learning and religious art. Aryabhata's calculations, surviving temples and a silk-weavers' inscription reveal knowledge and craft communities beyond the court. The empire fragmented by the middle of the sixth century, while cultural traditions continued.

fell.text: By around 550, repeated invasions and the independence of regional rulers had fragmented Gupta imperial power. This approximate endpoint describes a gradual political breakup, not one conquest or the disappearance of its communities.

summary: Mali connected West African gold-producing regions with a wider commercial and intellectual world. Mansa Musa became internationally famous through his pilgrimage, while architecture and oral performance preserved different forms of cultural memory.

Kush was an African kingdom of the Middle Nile whose centers included Napata and Meroe. Its rulers and craftspeople developed distinctive monuments while exchanging ideas with neighboring societies. The royal city, religious settlements and industrial remains show a civilization extending well beyond its famous pyramids.

Aksum linked the northern Ethiopian highlands to the Red Sea through Adulis. Its monuments and inscriptions reveal a kingdom connected to African and Mediterranean exchange networks. The city also retained religious and ceremonial importance after its political power diminished.

Ancient Egypt brought together royal power, skilled workshops and a durable written culture along the Nile. Its art changed substantially across the Old and Middle Kingdoms. Pyramids, family memorials and ordinary letters reveal different parts of that society; surviving evidence is often weighted toward elite tombs.

Punic Carthage grew into a major western Mediterranean trading and naval power. Its houses, writing, coins and sanitation reveal more than Hannibal’s wars. Rome destroyed the city in 146 BCE; a Roman city later rose on the site, while Punic traditions did not disappear with one capital.

Numidian society belongs to North Africa's indigenous history and its wider Mediterranean connections. Thugga, now Dougga, offers evidence for urban life under Numidian kings and for its transformation under Roman rule. The spectacular Roman monuments there are later additions to an older town.

The Almoravids governed from Marrakesh and connected Saharan routes with North African and Iberian towns. Their rule supported major religious buildings and crafts, while their capital helped shape the urban geography of the western Islamic world.

The Almohads made Marrakesh a center of government and learning while maintaining a major Iberian center at Seville. Monumental mosques, gates and city walls gave their rule an enduring architectural presence.

The Marinids made Fez a royal capital and sponsored an urban culture of learning, worship, commerce and craftsmanship. Their new town stood beside the older medina, creating a capital with complementary royal and civic spaces.

Under Hafsid rule, Tunis was a wealthy center of the western Islamic world. Its urban history joins markets, religious institutions and residential neighborhoods. The surviving medina contains work from several dynasties, so individual buildings require their own dates and patronage histories.

The medieval Soninke empire of Ghana prospered through trans-Saharan exchange. Its power rested on commercial connections and political centers such as Kumbi Saleh, rather than a fixed border enclosing one people.

Songhai's wealth linked Gao and the Niger region to trans-Saharan commerce. Its surviving monuments make construction, religious practice and shared maintenance visible alongside the better-known history of its rulers.
Benin's court commissioned brass sculpture to preserve royal memory and express authority. This Edo kingdom was centered in present-day Nigeria, distinct from the modern country named Benin.

Luba political life joined sacred kingship with council authority. Artworks could carry political knowledge, embody ancestral relationships, or serve highly practical purposes within elite daily life.

Lunda rulers adapted aspects of Luba kingship while maintaining their own political independence. Trade routes and relationships with neighboring courts supported the movement of materials, artistic forms and political ideas.

The Kuba kingdom brought together several principalities in Central Africa. Royal and aristocratic patronage encouraged inventive textiles, carved vessels and images through which rank and historical memory became visible.

Asante architecture joined construction skill with visual language and religious practice. Surviving shrine buildings near Kumasi preserve parts of a tradition that remained meaningful beyond the period of imperial power.

At Abomey, the royal palaces combined government, skilled craft production and the storage of royal treasures. Their architecture and imagery expressed Aja-Fon traditions and preserved memories of successive rulers.

Olmec names a group of early Mesoamerican societies, especially those of Mexico's Gulf Coast. Their monumental building projects and stoneworking joined local farming communities to far-reaching networks of materials and artistic ideas.

Maya history encompasses distinct societies and city-states. Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque and Copan supported royal courts with specialized artists; their political histories should be explored individually rather than compressed into one Maya empire.

Teotihuacan was a major urban center in central Mexico. Its public monuments, apartment compounds and specialized arts connected a large city with other Mesoamerican communities through exchange and influence.
Monte Alban was an important Zapotec capital in the Oaxaca Valley. Its history of urban planning, water management and carved inscriptions is one part of the much wider history of Zapotec societies.

Moche societies flourished along Peru's northern coastal valleys during the first through eighth centuries CE. Their ceramics preserve an unusually rich visual record of people, animals, plants and ritual activity.

The Chimu kingdom made Chan Chan a major center on Peru's north coast. Its earthen compounds, craft production and water systems show how a large city organized resources in a dry coastal environment.
Tenochtitlan brought canals, markets, workshops and ceremonial architecture into a large lake city. This card focuses on the capital's civic and artistic life within the Aztec imperial world.

Tawantinsuyu joined diverse Andean regions through roads, administration and local labor. Its infrastructure drew on earlier Andean traditions and adapted construction to mountains, valleys and coastal environments.

Pueblo societies comprise distinct communities and histories. Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde preserve ancestral building and farming landscapes; Taos Pueblo is a living community with its own traditions and government.

The Haudenosaunee are a continuing confederacy of nations. The Onondaga Nation's own accounts describe government, food, ceremonies and wampum as living practices connecting community responsibilities with historical memory.

Minoan is the modern name for Bronze Age Cretan culture, with several palatial centers rather than one securely documented island-wide kingdom. Its crafts, exchange networks and administrative writing linked Crete to the wider Mediterranean.
The Etruscans lived in a network of central Italian city-states. Metalworking, imported luxury materials and distinctive funerary art reveal communities deeply involved in Mediterranean exchange.

The Greek city-states formed a varied political and cultural world. These examples focus on Athens and Classical sculpture; Athenian institutions should not be assumed to describe every Greek community.

Carolingian rulers made learning, Christian worship and patronage part of imperial government. Their workshops and scholars adapted older traditions into books, buildings and objects that influenced medieval Europe.
The Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy used Ravenna as a royal center. Its surviving buildings and personal ornaments show both distinctive traditions and close engagement with the Roman world.
Wessex was a kingdom in southern England. Under Alfred, royal support for reading and translation linked learned texts with the skilled production of books and precious objects.
Mercia was a kingdom in central England. Large earthworks and the Staffordshire Hoard offer different views of its region: organized construction and highly skilled early medieval metalwork.
Northumbria joined the regions of Bernicia and Deira. Its royal centers and monasteries supported learning, manuscript production and religious networks reaching beyond northern Britain.

Frankish communities expressed wealth and identity through dress and skilled metalwork. The map's Frankish Kingdom record covers only part of a longer history and should not imply that Frankish culture began in 600.
Venice joined lagoon engineering to a far-reaching artistic culture. This chapter follows the city and its painters during the Renaissance; it does not yet cover the republic's entire history.

In late-sixteenth- and early-seventeenth-century Genoa, mercantile wealth reshaped streets, houses and hospitality. The Rolli palaces reveal how private residences served the republic's public business.
This chapter follows Portuguese architecture and learning from the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries, through Lisbon's Belem complex and Coimbra's colleges, laboratories and printing facilities.

Architecture and painting show different sides of Spain's sixteenth- and seventeenth-century culture: a royal monastery organized around worship and learning, and pictures shaped by observation and international exchange.

Seventeenth-century French projects joined engineering, landscape design and royal display. This chapter pairs a working waterway with Versailles to show different purposes of large-scale construction.

This chapter looks at scientific institutions in seventeenth-century England within the map's combined England-and-Ireland record. It also marks the later union of England and Scotland, which did not merge Ireland into Great Britain.
This chapter follows Renaissance planning and learning in Poland-Lithuania. Zamosc offers a local view of how architectural ideas, commerce and education could meet in one deliberately planned town.
Early-modern Sweden supported both industrial communities and elaborate court art. Falun's copper landscape and Drottningholm's theatre reveal very different kinds of skilled work.

This chapter follows sixteenth-century Denmark-Norway through astronomy, printing and royal architecture. Tycho Brahe's observatory shows how scientific work depended on buildings, instruments and supporting crafts.

This chapter follows the designed landscapes and museum ambitions associated with Prussia in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. It focuses on architects, craftspeople and the institutions that organized their work.

Twentieth-century Copenhagen became a meeting place for physicists working on quantum theory. This focused chapter follows the institute, discussions and everyday arrangements that helped international collaboration take root.
In the early twentieth century, Dutch engineers and designers experimented with ways to manage water and domestic space. This chapter pairs a steam pumping station with an adaptable family home.
Yolngu peoples maintain distinct clan identities in Arnhem Land. Country, law, food, ceremony and art remain connected, while institutions at Yirrkala carry knowledge through contemporary media.

Gunditjmara people maintain a living relationship with Country in south-western Victoria. At Budj Bim, generations shaped waterways into an aquaculture landscape. The map's imported date range describes its snapshots, not the beginning or end of Gunditjmara society.

Maori society comprises distinct iwi and hapu with their own histories and authority. This card introduces shared themes while preserving those differences. The imported map interval is not an extinction date: Maori communities, language and cultural institutions continue.

name: Māori
summary: Maori society comprises distinct iwi and hapu with their own histories and authority. This card introduces shared themes while preserving those differences. The imported map interval is not an extinction date: Maori communities, language and cultural institutions continue.

Kerma was the capital of a Nubian kingdom on the Nile in present-day Sudan. Its prosperity rested on herding, cultivation and exchange between African interiors and Egypt. This page follows the kingdom, its earlier background and what archaeology reveals about its people.
Great Zimbabwe was a stone-built center created by ancestors of the Shona. Its surviving walls preserve part of a larger settlement of homes, courtyards and monumental enclosures.

name: Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt
summary: A dynasty ruling from Alexandria as both Hellenistic monarchs and Egyptian pharaohs. Decrees, papyri, temples and art preserve its multilingual institutions and working communities.

name: Hawaiian Kingdom
summary: A Hawaiian monarchy with constitutional institutions, an active Hawaiian-language press and a rich cultural life. Fishponds, surviving newspapers and Iolani Palace reveal engineering, work and artistic traditions. The monarchy was overthrown in 1893.

Samoa connects a long Pacific history with enduring family institutions, skilled weaving and tattooing, and a struggle for independence. The western islands regained independence in 1962; Samoan communities also continue beyond that state.

Fiji brings together distinct iTaukei, Indo-Fijian and other community histories. Barkcloth, port buildings and labor records illuminate skilled production and colonial experience. Independence came in 1970, and cultural life continues in the islands and diaspora.

Monumental centers at Heketa and Lapaha, imported stone tools and finely made household objects illuminate the Tu'i Tonga chiefly world. Sacred rank and governing power changed across successive lines. The last Tu'i Tonga died in 1865; Tongan society continued.

Tonga's modern kingdom is known for continuing monarchy, parliamentary government, ngatu barkcloth and language-centered community life. A constitution and parliament emerged in 1875. British protected-state status ended in 1970, while Tongan cultural life continues at home and overseas.

American Samoa has deep traditions of stoneworking, siapo barkcloth and community knowledge. Its eastern islands entered a US territorial relationship through a contested period of partition and separate cessions. Naval administration ended in 1951; Samoan cultural life and local institutions continue.

name: Gunaikurnai
summary: Gunaikurnai communities connect Gippsland Country with clan relationships, stoneworking, cultural fire and living knowledge. Colonial displacement disrupted access and families; community life continues, including native title recognition in 2010.

name: Wurundjeri
summary: Wurundjeri history connects greenstone quarrying, community leadership, William Barak's art and living care for Birrarung. Colonial dispossession disrupted access to Country; descendants maintain and renew cultural responsibilities.

name: Wadawurrung
summary: Wadawurrung history includes stone arrangements, fishing technology, plant knowledge and living art across Country around Geelong and Ballarat. Colonization transformed access and ecosystems; the people and their cultural responsibilities continue.

name: Ngarrindjeri
summary: Ngarrindjeri communities connect the lower Murray, lakes, Coorong and Sea Country through fishing, kinship, law and creative practice. Feather flowers, weaving and David Unaipon's papers illuminate skill and adaptation; cultural life continues despite dispossession and environmental damage.

Vanuatu's island histories include Lapita settlement, chiefly landscapes, sand drawing and community research. The Anglo-French Condominium ended with independence in 1980; diverse cultural traditions and institutions continue.

Solomon Islands connects diverse island histories through canoe building, feather and shell valuables, music and exchange. British protectorate rule ended with independence in 1978, while regional communities and creative practices continue.

Aotearoa New Zealand's history includes Māori settlement and carving, colonial dispossession, women's voting campaigns, refrigerated exports and state housing. Independence developed through constitutional steps; the state and its communities continue.

Buganda's history joins royal councils with barkcloth, Kasubi's plant-based architecture and generations of musicians. Its restored royal institution has a cultural role in Uganda; Baganda communities continue.

Bunyoro's history includes Kibiro's salt gardens and pottery, regional exchange and Empaako naming. Colonial conquest, abolition of kingship and its cultural restoration changed institutions while Banyoro communities continued.

Caddo communities built river-valley settlements, farmed, traveled by canoe and made distinctive pottery. Dispossession forced major movements, while the Caddo Nation and cultural traditions continue.

Cherokee histories include Sequoyah's writing system, bilingual newspapers, basketry and living food knowledge. Forced removal devastated communities, which rebuilt and continue through distinct Cherokee nations.

Muscogee histories connect ancestral Ocmulgee, town councils and kinship with later institutions at Okmulgee. Forced removal transformed political geography; Muscogee communities and the Nation continue.

name: Nova Scotia peninsula (British rule)
summary: Britain governed peninsular Nova Scotia after 1713, within a region already home to Mi’kmaq communities and Acadian settlements.

name: Accomac communities
summary: Indigenous Accomac communities occupied Virginia’s southern Eastern Shore, farming, fishing and exchanging goods across its creeks and coastal landscapes.

name: Gold Coast (British colony)
summary: British coastal colony, administered alongside Ashanti, the Northern Territories and British Togoland.

name: Gold Coast colony (Accra)
summary: British coastal colony, administered alongside Ashanti, the Northern Territories and British Togoland.

name: Gold Coast and associated territories
summary: British coastal colony, administered alongside Ashanti, the Northern Territories and British Togoland.

name: Adena culture (misdated map record)
summary: Adena is an archaeological label for early Woodland communities in the Ohio River region. This imported 1492 to 1500 record is chronologically misplaced; its interval does not establish a culture or kingdom at that date.

name: Ahé (Karipuna of Rondônia)
summary: Ahé, also known as the Karipuna of Rondônia, are a Tupi-Kawahib people of the Jacy-Paraná and Mutum-Paraná region in Brazil. Their communities continue despite devastating contact and territorial invasion.

name: Akaitcho Dene
summary: Akaitcho Dene communities around Great Slave Lake include the Yellowknives Dene, Łutsël K’é Dene and Deninu K’ue First Nations, with distinct local histories and continuing institutions.

name: Alabama people
summary: The Alabama are an Indigenous people whose earlier homes lay in what is now Alabama. Communities later established homes farther west; the Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas preserves a shared political history with the closely associated Coushatta people.

name: Regency of Algiers
summary: The Regency of Algiers governed from the port under Ottoman affiliation. French forces took Algiers in 1830, ending the dey’s government. The city and its communities continued under colonial rule.

name: Alsea people
summary: The Alsea are an Indigenous people of the central Oregon coast, including the Alsea River and Cape Perpetua area. Their history includes coastal food gathering, language and storytelling, forced displacement and continuing community life.

name: Amazonian societies (regional overview)
summary: A broad regional map category covering diverse Amazonian histories. Named archaeological sites reveal forest and river foraging, early cultivation, pottery and later earthworks; they do not define a single people or state.

The Arabela are an Indigenous people of Loreto in Peru. Their history includes river and forest livelihoods, forced labour, changing settlements and continuing efforts to document and teach their language.

name: Puerto Rico
summary: This outline represents Puerto Rico under Spanish rule in the eighteenth century. Its imported label incorrectly named the Danish Virgin Islands, a different island group farther east. The displayed dates describe this map snapshot, not Puerto Rico's historical lifetime.

name: Saint-Domingue
summary: French Saint-Domingue occupied western Hispaniola before Haitian independence in 1804. The map’s 1715 to 1783 interval is only a slice of this history.
Surinam is an older spelling associated here with the colonial territory on South America’s northern coast. English settlement from 1650 was followed by Dutch conquest in 1667.
This map record depicts Suriname under Dutch colonial government. Its 1878 to 1914 interval is a map window, not the colony’s full history.
French Guiana is a territory of France in northeastern South America. Its history includes colonial administration, departmental status and the combined territorial institutions established in 2016.
The Assiniboine are a living Indigenous people with communities in the United States and Canada, including Fort Peck and Carry the Kettle Nakoda Nation.
The Assiniboine are a living Indigenous people with communities in the United States and Canada, including Fort Peck and Carry the Kettle Nakoda Nation.

Arapaho people continue in distinct northern and southern communities, including the Northern Arapaho Tribe at Wind River in Wyoming and Southern Arapaho members of the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes in Oklahoma.
Alwa was a medieval kingdom centred on Soba on the Blue Nile in present-day Sudan. Its capital housed royal and church institutions, workshops and communities connected to distant exchange networks.

Makkura is a name for Makuria, the medieval Nubian kingdom whose capital was Dongola, also called Tungul. Excavated houses, churches, workshops and texts reveal a city on the Nile in present-day Sudan.

The Funj Sultanate ruled from Sennar in present-day Sudan. It developed in the early sixteenth century and lost independence to Turco-Egyptian conquest in 1821. The map shows separate snapshots of this history.

Botswana became an independent republic on 30 September 1966, after British rule as the Bechuanaland Protectorate. Earlier map entries cover the same territory before independence; their dates do not mark the birth or disappearance of its communities.

Lesotho became independent from Britain on 4 October 1966. Its earlier colonial name was Basutoland. The separate map records cover parts of a continuing regional history, rather than three unrelated countries.

Swaziland became independent from Britain on 6 September 1968. The country adopted the name Eswatini in 2018. These map records cover parts of one continuing regional history, including years before independence.

Mozambique became independent from Portugal on 25 June 1975. Portuguese East Africa and the later Mozambique map records cover different parts of this regional history, including colonial years; their starting dates are not dates of national independence.

Northern Rhodesia became independent from Britain as Zambia on 24 October 1964. The map’s Zambia records begin earlier, in 1920 and 1960, so those dates describe coverage of the territory rather than the founding of the independent republic.

Zimbabwe became independent on 18 April 1980. These map records also cover earlier Southern Rhodesia, including company administration, colonial minority rule and the disputed Rhodesian declaration of 1965. Their starting years, 1920 and 1960, are map coverage dates rather than the republic’s founding.

Malawi became independent from Britain on 6 July 1964 and a republic two years later. The map record begins in 1920, when the territory was called Nyasaland, so its starting year describes map coverage rather than the birth of the independent country.

This page follows Madagascar as an island region across different political periods. France annexed it in 1896, and independence was proclaimed on 26 June 1960. The map’s separate intervals are not the beginning or ending of the island’s communities.

The Merina kingdom grew from Madagascar’s central highlands. Andrianampoinimerina consolidated power in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries through war, trade and family connections. The map’s early starting date does not establish that this kingdom existed in the year 1000.

The Merina kingdom grew from Madagascar’s central highlands. Andrianampoinimerina consolidated power in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries through war, trade and family connections. The map’s early starting date does not establish that this kingdom existed in the year 1000.

Malagasy peoples have histories connecting Madagascar with eastern Africa and Southeast Asia. Communities across the island have distinct traditions and shared connections. The map’s 800 to 1000 interval is a coverage window, not the lifetime of a people or a kingdom.
Zanzibar’s Swahili trading towns, royal court and plantations had distinct histories. The map’s 1715 to 1914 coverage is not the separate sultanate’s lifetime.

name: Sultanate of Zanzibar
summary: Zanzibar’s Swahili trading towns, royal court and plantations had distinct histories. The map’s 1715 to 1914 coverage is not the separate sultanate’s lifetime.

The Roman Republic grew from a city-state into a Mediterranean power. The map shows selected centuries of that history; Caesar’s assassination in 44 BCE and the Augustan settlement in 27 BCE mark different steps in its political ending.

The western imperial court governed from Italy while authority elsewhere changed unevenly. Odoacer removed Romulus Augustulus in 476, but Roman communities and eastern imperial rule continued. The map’s 400 to 500 CE polygon is not a precise political lifetime.

Punic Carthage grew into a major western Mediterranean trading and naval power. Its houses, writing, coins and sanitation reveal more than Hannibal’s wars. Rome destroyed the city in 146 BCE; a Roman city later rose on the site, while Punic traditions did not disappear with one capital.

The people of the eastern Roman Empire called themselves Romans. From Constantinople they governed a changing realm for more than a millennium, building domes and walls, copying books, caring for children and debating faith. The imperial capital fell to the Ottomans in 1453, while its communities and traditions continued.

For centuries, the Holy Roman Empire linked many central European rulers, towns and communities under an elected emperor. Its borders and powers changed, while workshops, schools, printing presses and households shaped life beyond the court. Francis II gave up the imperial crown in 1806; the people and their cultures continued.

From an Anatolian frontier principality, the Ottomans built an empire spanning parts of Europe, Asia and Africa. Their subjects spoke many languages and maintained diverse faiths, while markets, schools, baths, workshops and households shaped daily life. Expansion, reform and violence marked different centuries. The sultanate ended in 1922; its peoples and cultural traditions continued.

Peter I adopted the imperial title in 1721, and the Romanov state grew into a vast, diverse empire across Europe and Asia. Its cities, farms, schools, workshops and railways changed unevenly; serfdom and colonial rule shaped many lives. Nicholas II abdicated in 1917 amid war and revolution. The monarchy ended, while its peoples, languages and places continued.

The United States declared independence in 1776 and built a federal republic. Its history includes Indigenous sovereignty and forced removal, slavery and emancipation, migration, industry, struggles for equal rights, science and changing daily life. Families and communities have never shared one experience. The state continues today, so the map shows changing periods rather than a single ending.

The German Empire united German states under a Prussian king as emperor in 1871. It grew into an industrial and scientific power, but class divisions, colonial violence and political exclusions shaped its rule. Workers and families lived far from the palace image. Defeat and revolution ended the imperial monarchy in 1918; German people and communities continued.

Austria-Hungary formed a dual monarchy in 1867 under the Habsburg ruler. Its many languages and communities, two governments, cities and countryside made it more than a single culture. Daily life ranged from crowded workers' rooms to multilingual schools and court service. War and competing national movements brought the monarchy to an end in 1918; its peoples and traditions continued.

The map’s early “United Kingdom” slice begins after England and Scotland formed Great Britain in 1707 and runs through the 1801 union with Ireland. It covers industrial growth and an expanding empire as well as enslavement, Irish famine, crowded homes and unequal political rights. The 1878 map cutoff is only a snapshot boundary; Britain continued.

The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland began in 1801. Industrial power and imperial reach grew, while slavery, famine, inequality and demands for Irish self-government shaped its people’s lives. Most of Ireland became the Irish Free State in 1922; the formal royal and parliamentary title changed in 1927. The state and its people continued under a different territorial name.

The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland is a continuing state. Its twentieth- and twenty-first-century history includes world war, the NHS, migration, the end of most colonial rule, devolved government and many living languages. The map’s 1938 start is a snapshot date, not the country’s founding.

The Soviet Union was a multi-republic state founded in 1922. It industrialized rapidly, expanded schooling and healthcare and launched the first satellite and human spaceflight, while forced collectivization, famine, purges and wartime devastation caused immense suffering. Homes, languages and opportunities differed across republics. The union dissolved in 1991; its peoples and cultures continued in independent countries.

Canada formed as a federation in 1867 from four British North American provinces and expanded across lands long home to First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples. Its history includes treaties, railways, immigration, insulin research and public health insurance, alongside residential schools and racist exclusions. Family, school and language experiences vary greatly. Canada continues; the map’s 1815 start predates Confederation.

Brazil became an independent empire in 1822 and a republic in 1889; the imported map begins only in 1878. Its history includes slavery and abolition, industrial growth, public-health research, two dictatorships and the 1988 constitution. Indigenous and quilombola communities, many languages and regional cultural practices continue. Brazil remains a republic; changing governments did not end its peoples or state.

Mexico won independence in 1821 and established a federal republic in 1824, well before the imported 1878 map snapshot. Railways and the long Díaz presidency preceded the 1910 revolution and 1917 constitution; education, land and labor rights changed amid conflict. Indigenous communities and languages, everyday maize traditions, worker health insurance and electoral change are part of its continuing history. Mexico remains a republic.

The Kingdom of Italy formed in 1861 and took Rome in 1870, before the imported map begins in 1878. Mass emigration and expanding schools marked the kingdom; Fascist dictatorship, colonial war and antisemitic laws brought grave harm. Italy became a republic by referendum in 1946, wrote a new constitution and later established public national health care. Family life changed with industrial migration and household technology, while minority languages continued. Italy remains a republic.

The Russian Federation emerged from the Soviet breakup in 1991, three years before the imported map begins. It continued the Soviet UN seat and adopted a constitution in 1993. Market transition caused hardship, Chechen wars harmed civilians, and Russian-built hardware helped begin the space station. Its 2014 claim to Crimea was rejected by the UN General Assembly, which also demanded withdrawal after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. Russia continues with many peoples and languages.

This imported “Germany” record covers 1878-1945, spanning the German Empire, Weimar Republic and Nazi dictatorship rather than one unchanging regime. Industrial growth and public health reforms changed homes; war, 1923 inflation and the Holocaust brought terrible harm. Nazi Germany launched European war and murdered six million Jews and millions of others. The regime collapsed in 1945 and occupation followed, while German people continued. Separate cards cover the Empire and postwar German states.

Germany reunited on 3 October 1990 when the German Democratic Republic joined the Federal Republic; the imported map begins only in 1994. The 1949 Basic Law and its human-dignity principle continued. Families had to navigate changed jobs, schools, health systems and homes, while migration gave Germany many languages and communities. A 2022 census still tracks home toilets and baths separately. Germany continues as a federal republic, and the earlier East and West histories remain distinct.

East Germany, the German Democratic Republic, existed from 7 October 1949 to 3 October 1990. The imported 1960 to 1994 map interval begins late and ends after reunification. SED rule restricted elections and travel, while work, childcare, prefab homes, school clubs and holiday camps shaped everyday life. Indoor bathrooms and medical care differed across homes and years. Peaceful protest and a free 1990 election led to the GDR joining the Federal Republic; its people and family histories continued.

West Germany refers to the Federal Republic of Germany during the 1949 to 1990 division. Its Basic Law, parliament and statutory health insurance shaped a democracy that continued after unification. Postwar housing shortages gave way to construction and consumer goods for many, though gains were unequal. Migrant workers and their families also built West German society. In 1990 the GDR joined the Federal Republic: the Cold War name West Germany ended, but the Federal Republic did not.

The Viceroyalty of New Spain was established in 1535 and ruled from Mexico City until independence in 1821. Its historic jurisdiction included much more than modern Mexico; the imported polygon covers only about 1530 to 1715 and is not a complete border history. Indigenous, African, Spanish and mixed communities lived under unequal colonial laws while making their own families, art, petitions, foods and languages. Silver linked Acapulco to Asia, and Indigenous knowledge shaped medicine. Mexico inherited most, but not all, of the viceroyalty in 1821.

aliases: Republic of the Seven United Netherlands
summary: The Dutch Republic was a confederation of seven provinces from 1588 until the Batavian Revolution of 1795. The imported map covers only about 1600 to 1783. Its merchants, printers, painters and scholars flourished, while overseas companies used violence and slavery in Asia, Africa and the Americas. Families worked, learned, played and coped with household chores and illness very differently by wealth and place. The old republic ended politically in 1795; Dutch people and communities continued through the Batavian Republic and later states.

The Austrian Empire was created in 1804 under the Habsburgs and reorganized as Austria-Hungary in 1867. The imported “austrian-empire” map label spans about 1650 to 1878, so it includes earlier Habsburg lands and later Dual Monarchy years beyond this particular regime. The empire was multilingual and socially unequal. Schools, middle-class parlors, water supply and Vienna hospital hygiene show changing daily life alongside the 1848 revolutions. The 1867 compromise changed its government; its many people and communities continued.

aliases: United Kingdoms of Sweden and Norway
summary: Sweden and Norway shared a monarch from 1814 to 1905, while Norway retained its own constitution and parliament. The imported “sweden-norway” map interval runs from about 1815 to 1914, but the union ended in 1905. Households ranged from farms to growing towns; children helped with chores, schooling expanded unevenly, and disease and sanitation remained everyday concerns. Norwegian parliamentarianism, language and cultural movements, and disputes over foreign affairs shaped the end of the union. Sami people faced coercive language policy. Norway and Sweden separated through negotiation in 1905.
